content: Tuberculosis (TB) is a significant cause of illness and mortality in children living with HIV in regions where TB is highly prevalent. While it is well-established that isoniazid prophylaxis can prevent TB in HIV-negative children who have been exposed to TB, its effectiveness in preventing TB in HIV-positive children remains uncertain. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of TB preventive treatment with isoniazid compared to placebo in HIV-positive children who had no known contact with active TB. The outcomes assessed included the incidence of active TB, mortality, and any reported adverse events. To gather evidence, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, and two trial registries, up to February 2017. The analysis included randomized controlled trials involving HIV-positive children, both with and without known TB exposure, who were assigned to receive either isoniazid prophylaxis or a placebo. Three trials were included in the analysis, involving a total of 991 children under the age of 13 from South Africa and Botswana. Participants were randomized to receive isoniazid prophylaxis or placebo, administered either daily or three times weekly. The median follow-up period ranged from 5.7 to 34 months. Some of the children were receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) during the study. In HIV-positive children who were not on ART, isoniazid prophylaxis appeared to reduce the risk of developing active TB (hazard ratio [HR] 0.31, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.11 to 0.87; based on one trial with 240 participants, low-certainty evidence). Additionally, isoniazid prophylaxis may reduce the risk of death in this group (HR 0.46, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.95; based on one trial with 240 participants, low-certainty evidence). One trial involving 182 participants reported laboratory adverse events, which were similar between the isoniazid and placebo groups. No clinical adverse events were reported in this group. In HIV-positive children who were on ART, the evidence did not demonstrate a clear benefit of isoniazid prophylaxis in reducing the risk of active TB (risk ratio [RR] 0.76, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.14; based on three trials with 737 participants, very low-certainty evidence) or death (RR 1.45, 95% CI 0.78 to 2.72; based on three trials with 737 participants, very low-certainty evidence). Two trials involving 714 participants reported clinical adverse events, and three trials involving 795 participants reported laboratory adverse events. In both categories, the number of adverse events was similar between the isoniazid and placebo groups. In conclusion, isoniazid prophylaxis may reduce the risk of active TB and mortality in HIV-positive children who are not on ART, based on studies conducted in Africa. However, in HIV-positive children who are on ART, no clear benefit of isoniazid prophylaxis was observed.
